introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination / Technical and Vocational Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2020. Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
This question refers to the table below which shows the relationship between the annual rates of change in the general price level and the annual rates of change in unemployment of a given country.

| Annual rates of change in the general price level (%) | Annual rates of change in unemployment (%) |
|---|---|
| 40 | 5 |
| 35 | 6 |
| 30 | 8 |
| 25 | 10 |
| 20 | 13 |
| 15 | 17 |
| 10 | 21 |
| 5 | 26 |
| 0 | 35 |
| -5 | 40 |

figures.legende: Phillips curve plotted from the table (unemployment on the horizontal axis, rate of change of the price level on the vertical axis), with the long-run Phillips curve drawn vertically at the NAIRU, read at 35% where inflation is zero (model answer to Q4(a)(i) and (c)).

incertitudes: Question 4 : le tableau est imprimé tel quel (taux de variation des prix de 40 à -5 %, taux de variation du chômage de 5 à 40 %). Les valeurs sont irréalistes (35 % de chômage pour une inflation nulle) : elles sont recopiées sans les corriger. Le sujet ne dit pas quel axe porte quelle variable ; le corrigé place le chômage en abscisse et l'inflation en ordonnée (convention de la courbe de Phillips) et l'indique.

Question 4(c) : le sujet ne précise pas l'inflation anticipée. Le NAIRU est lu à l'intersection de la courbe avec l'axe horizontal (inflation nulle, soit 35 % de chômage sur ces données), complété par la courbe de Phillips de long terme verticale ; c'est une lecture, le sujet n'imprimant pas de valeur.
Question 4(a)(i) : la figure du corrigé est un modèle du graphique demandé au candidat (produit avec matplotlib à partir des dix couples du tableau).

Aucun total n'est imprimé par question (« All questions carry equal marks ») : `points` de l'exercice est laissé vide ; les points de chaque sous-question (a), (b)... sont la somme des points imprimés de ses parties ; la somme des points imprimés de la question vaut 20.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Using a graph paper, plot the information from the above table. (4 marks)

(ii) What name is given the curve in (a)(i) above? (2 marks)

(iii) State the relationship that exists between these two variables as depicted by the curve. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Plotting.** Draw a graph with the **annual rate of unemployment (%) on the horizontal axis** (scale 0 to 40, say 1 cm for 5%) and the **annual rate of change in the general price level, i.e. the rate of inflation (%), on the vertical axis** (scale -5 to 40). Label both axes and give the graph a title. Plot the ten pairs (unemployment, inflation): (5, 40), (6, 35), (8, 30), (10, 25), (13, 20), (17, 15), (21, 10), (26, 5), (35, 0), (40, -5), and join the points with a smooth curve. The curve slopes **downwards from left to right** and is convex to the origin (steep at low unemployment, flatter at high unemployment). It crosses the horizontal axis at 35% unemployment. (If the axes are interchanged the marks are still given when the labelling is consistent.)

![fig-1](gce-al-economics-2020-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_4_fig_1.png)

**(ii) Name of the curve.** It is the **Phillips curve** (the short-run Phillips curve).

**(iii) Relationship.** The curve shows an **inverse (negative) relationship, or trade-off, between inflation and unemployment**: when the rate of inflation is high the rate of unemployment is low, and when inflation falls unemployment rises. For example, on the table inflation of 40% goes with 5% unemployment, while inflation of 0% goes with 35% unemployment. A government that wants lower unemployment must therefore accept higher inflation, and vice versa.

questions.enonce_markdown: Define the natural rate of unemployment (NAIRU). (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: The **natural rate of unemployment** is the **rate of unemployment that exists when the labour market is in equilibrium**, that is, when the number of workers seeking jobs equals the number of vacancies at the going real wage, so that actual inflation equals expected inflation. It consists of frictional, structural and seasonal unemployment (but no demand-deficient unemployment). **NAIRU** stands for the **Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment**: it is the unemployment rate at which inflation neither accelerates nor decelerates. Any attempt to push unemployment below it by expanding demand only raises inflation in the long run.

questions.enonce_markdown: On the graph in a(i) above, indicate NAIRU. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: The natural rate (NAIRU) is shown by the point where the Phillips curve meets the horizontal axis, where the rate of change of prices is zero (expected inflation is nil, so actual inflation equals expected inflation), and by a **vertical line drawn through that point: the long-run Phillips curve**. On the data of the table the curve cuts the horizontal axis at **35% unemployment**, so the NAIRU is read as 35% (the vertical dashed line in the figure above, labelled NAIRU). Whatever the rate of inflation, in the long run unemployment returns to this level, so there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Enumerate:

(i) four benefits of inflation to an economy. (4 marks)

(ii) four costs of unemployment to society. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Four benefits of (mild) inflation to an economy** (1 mark each, any four):

1. **Encourages investment and output** - when prices rise faster than costs, profit margins rise, which stimulates firms to produce and invest.
2. **Reduces the real burden of debt** - borrowers (households, firms and the government) repay in money that has lost value, so debts are easier to service.
3. **Lower unemployment in the short run** - as the Phillips curve shows, higher inflation is associated with lower unemployment, because firms hire more workers to meet rising demand.
4. **Higher nominal tax revenue for the government**, since nominal incomes and spending rise, and **it avoids the problems of deflation** (postponed spending, falling output).
5. It makes it easier to adjust relative prices and real wages across sectors, because workers resist nominal wage cuts.

**(ii) Four costs of unemployment to society** (1 mark each, any four):

1. **Loss of output** - labour is a wasted resource, so the economy operates inside its production possibilities frontier and national income is lower.
2. **Loss of income and lower living standards** for the unemployed and their dependants, leading to poverty and inequality.
3. **Cost to the government** - more spending on unemployment benefits and social support, and lower income tax and VAT revenue.
4. **Social costs** - crime, family breakdown, ill health and stress, rural-urban drift and discontent.
5. **Loss of skills (deskilling)** - long-term unemployed workers lose their skills and become less employable.
